summary: This note is an excerpt from the NCBI Bookshelf edition of 'Psychological Testing in the Service of Disability Determination,' a 2015 National Academies Press report by an Institute of Medicine committee, specifically Chapter 3, 'Overview of Psychological Testing.' It explains how psychological assessment gathers information from records, interviews, observations, corroborative informants and formal tests, and it classifies tests by what they measure, how they are administered and scored, and how results are normed. It also introduces psychometric concepts of reliability, validity and standardization, noting that the committee does not recommend any specific test. The web page navigation and account boilerplate were ignored.
one_line: Chapter 3 of a 2015 National Academies report introduces psychological testing types, psychometric properties, and norms used in disability determination.
key_facts: The report 'Psychological Testing in the Service of Disability Determination' was published by National Academies Press (US) on 2015 Jun 29.
Psychological assessment gathers information about an individual through records, interviews, behavioral observations, corroborative interviews and formal testing.
The clinical interview is described as the foundation of many psychological and neuropsychological assessments.
Tests of typical behavior (often non-cognitive measures) are distinguished from tests of maximal performance (often cognitive tests).
The best predictor of intelligence test performance is described as one's vocabulary.
Nonverbal measures were given as intelligence tests for non-English speaking soldiers in the United States as early as World War I.
In norm-referenced scoring, a test-taker at the 60th percentile has scored better than 60 percent of the norm group.
Criterion-referenced tests compare a score to a fixed standard, such as a driving test where one only passes or fails.
Reliability is described as the degree to which scores from a test are stable and results are consistent.
Validity is defined as 'the degree to which evidence and theory support the interpretations of test scores for proposed uses of tests' (AERA et al., 2014, p. 11).
The report notes that validity refers to the interpretation and use of test scores, not to the test itself.
Three traditional types of validity evidence are construct, content, and criterion-related validity.
Standardization includes a quiet, relatively distraction-free environment, precise reading of scripted instructions, and provision of necessary tools or stimuli.
The committee refrains from recommending the use of any specific test; references to specific tests are illustrative examples only.
